francis-of-assisi.history:
St. Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan Order, was born at Assisi in Umbria in 1181 or 1182, the exact year being uncertain. His father, Pietro Bernardone, was a wealthy cloth merchant; of his mother, Pica, little is known, though she is said to have belonged to a noble family of Provence. Baptized Giovanni, the child was renamed Francesco by his father, apparently out of fondness for France. The legend that he was born in a stable arose only in the fifteenth century.

As a youth Francis received elementary instruction from the priests of St. George's at Assisi, but he was not studious, and his literary education remained incomplete. Though associated with his father in trade, he showed little liking for a merchant's career. His early life gave no presage of sanctity: he loved pleasure, sang merrily, and delighted in fine clothes, becoming the favourite of the young nobles of Assisi and the leader of its revels. Yet even then he showed an instinctive sympathy with the poor.

At about twenty he rode out with the townsmen against Perugia, was taken prisoner, and was held captive for more than a year. A low fever contracted there appears to have turned his thoughts to eternal things, yet with returning health his eagerness for glory reawakened, and he prepared to join Walter of Brienne, then in arms in the Neapolitan States. A dream of a vast hall hung with armour all marked with the Cross, and a second illness at Spoleto followed by another dream bidding him return at once, sent him back to Assisi in 1205.

His demeanour changed, though he still joined at times in the revels of his former comrades. Asked jestingly whether he meant to marry, he answered that he was about to take a wife of surpassing fairness: Lady Poverty, whom Dante and Giotto later wedded to his name. He gave up his gay attire and wasteful ways, seeking in prayer and solitude the meaning of his call. Meeting a poor leper on the Umbrian plain, he overcame his instinctive disgust, dismounted, embraced the man, and gave him all the money he had. On a pilgrimage to Rome he emptied his purse at the tomb of St. Peter and, having exchanged clothes with a tattered mendicant, stood fasting that day among the beggars at the basilica door.

While praying before an ancient crucifix in the forsaken wayside chapel of St. Damian's below the town, he heard a voice saying, 'Go, Francis, and repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.' Taking the words literally, he sold horse and drapery at Foligno to raise money for the church's restoration; when the priest refused the gold, he flung it from him. His father's wrath drove him to hide for a month in a cave near San Damiano, and when he emerged, emaciated and squalid, he was pelted with mud and stones and mocked as a madman. In time Francis renounced his inheritance, embraced poverty, and gave himself to repairing churches and serving lepers.

Followers gradually gathered around him and became the Order of Friars Minor; with St. Clare he inspired the community known as the Poor Clares. He preached to all creatures: tradition holds that he preached to the birds and tamed a wolf. In 1224 he is said to have received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ. His Canticle of the Sun praises God through creation.

Francis died at the Porziuncola near Assisi on 3 October 1226 and was canonized in 1228. In the centuries since, a vast literature has grown up around him; modern study has recovered important early texts and has re-edited and translated his own writings. His feast is kept on 4 October, and he is venerated as the patron of animals and ecology.
